blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this KDD'17 paper as an insightful case study into Leicester City's unexpected 2015/16 Premier League title win, using advanced soccer analytics. The paper goes beyond traditional metrics like shots on target to develop a strategic gameplay features model that proves useful in predicting game outcomes. Colyer notes that while Leicester's counter-attacking style was often cited as the reason for their success, the real key was their defensive effectiveness—particularly through goalkeeping, defensive strategy, and pass disruption. The authors demonstrate how machine learning models trained on shot and pass data can reveal nuanced performance insights, with Leicester's goalkeeper Kasper Schmeichel accounting for a significant portion of their goal differential. The paper also shows how these strategic features can be used to build predictive models and even a recommendation engine for pre-game preparation, bridging descriptive analytics with practical predictive value.
paper_title: The Leicester City Fairytale? Utilizing new soccer analytics tools to compare performance in the 15/16 and 16/17 EPL seasons
paper_abstract: �e last two years has been somewhat of a rollercoaster for English Premier League (EPL) team Leicester City. In the 2015/16 season, against all odds and logic, they won the league to much fan-fare. Fast-forward nine months later, and they are ba�ling relegation. What could describe this �uctuating form? As soccer is a very complex and strategic game, common statistics (e.g., passes, shots, possession) do not really tell the full story on how a team succeeds and fails. However, using machine learning tools and a plethora of data, it is now possible to obtain some insights into how a team performs. To showcase the utility of these new tools (i.e., expected goal value, expected save value, strategy-plots and passing quality measures), we �rst analyze the EPL 2015-16 season which a speci�c emphasis on the champions Leicester City. We then compare their performance in that season to the current one (16/17). Finally, we show how these features can be used predict future performance.
